body_markdown:
As touched on previously in this space, TV and film productions sometimes say they want to “double” a car—that is, find an exact or very close match. The reasons for doing so vary. On some occasions, it’s more economical to film two different scenes in two different places at the same time, necessitating a second matching car. Other times, production wants a double because they anticipate significant alterations. As in, they expect to run the risk of—or indeed plan on—damaging the double, say, in a crash or near-crash scene. Or the plan might be to modify a car less brutally by welding receiver hitches to as many as six points on its bottom-side perimeter, into which camera rigging might be mounted for certain key shots (in the cost-no-object eyes of the director).


Unsurprisingly, few people want their cars to be modified like this or wrecked. Which brings us at Octane Film Cars to a not infrequent type of job in which we are asked to find and purchase a double and lease it to the production under what’s known as “rent to wreck” agreement. It doesn’t mean the car will *actually* be wrecked, or even visibly altered. The car may come back fine and untouched, but these deals tend to be long-lease situations (life of a series, in some instances) and it’s cheaper and less hassle for the production to buy than renting the double for a long period or being on the hook for any damages on set, which they are with standard rentals.


Jamie Kitman


That’s the context concerning a recent request we received to search for a W205-generation Mercedes-Benz C300 4Matic that would match a car already being used by a production we’re working on. I happen to be a particular fan of these C300s, which ran from 2015-2021. It’s why we suggested it as the recurrent “hero” car in the first place. Though of relatively recent vintage, it’s a modern throwback to the days when Mercedes’ bank-vault solidity was indisputable, before a rough patch late in the last century saw an over-enthusiastic cost-cutting drive that led to the occasional blip in legendary Benz quality. The W205 C-Class proved, as much as anything, that the company had convincingly relocated its mojo—not just to come roaring back with a machine liberated from rattles and electronic bugs, but also one that was a sporty delight to drive. Blessed with surefooted handling, an exceptional ride, and admirable body control, plus brisk acceleration thanks to a turbocharged four-cylinder with fuel economy that nips at 40 mpg on the highway. Buying a used one ought to have been a pleasure, and in the end it was, but we’re here to talk about gratification delayed.


CarGurus


Because time was short, and on account of the rough life ahead, the car we were looking for didn’t have to be a low-mileage cream puff like you’d buy if you were keeping it for your own use. I checked online for nearby dealers. Lo and behold, just what we needed turned up on a website at a dealership in nearby Carlstadt, New Jersey. Purchase experience-wise, I didn’t expect much. To be fair, though I’ve met many reputable and trustworthy used car dealers in New Jersey, I’d met more who do not honor the state’s sterling reputation for fair trading and honest dealing. I spent my formative years in the Garden State, after all, and for lack of anything better to do would often peruse the forlorn and seedy lots lining Route 46 near Hackensack and Little Ferry, looking for unlikely gems in the rough. I met some characters who belonged behind bars, along with many who looked and smelled like they’d spent their life in front of bars.


I also vividly remember passing on a 1969 Shelby Cobra 500KR convertible a friend and I spotted at a lot in Ridgefield, New Jersey, across the street from the ShopRite supermarket where I worked the summer of my fifteenth year. The salesman wanted $900 for it. That was, alas, $750 more than I was worth, and when a punched out taillight on this otherwise fine-looking bargain turned out not to warrant the $350 discount I demanded, I was sent packing. Point is, I understand that some customers can be difficult, too. But these guys selling the Benz we needed were a whole other can of peas.


Mobility Global, Inc./Carfax


The online ad noted an asking price of $10,995. With a clean-ish Carfax and moderately high miles, some light work could be assumed, but it was within our budget. I called, said we were interested and asked whether there was any flex in the price. “Sure,” the guy I spoke to said (actually the third guy I spoke to, each one of whom initially had trouble identifying the car I was asking about, but each finally confirming that it was on the premises). We’re good to pay $10,500 today, I explained. “Well,” he replied, “we don’t negotiate on the phone. Come in and we’ll make a deal.” Fair enough. So, while I waded through some unrelated paperwork at my desk, I sent our trusty mechanic and savvy car buyer Bill Metzdorf to head right over and close the deal.


But when Bill got there 45 minutes later, they made him wait while they went to find the car. When it showed up fifteen minutes later, it looked good enough for our purposes. But when it came time to discuss the price and Bill suggested the modest discount I’d requested, they said it was non-negotiable. Worse still, the price was actually $13,500 plus registration and sales tax. Stunned, Bill got me, a lawyer, on the phone with the salesman. I tried again for the next fifteen minutes, but he wouldn’t budge. Along the way, the salesman explained matter-of-factly that this grossly inflated number included a mandatory “certification” fee, which their ad didn’t reference. What’s that? I asked. “It means it’s certified.” Yes, so you said, meaning… what exactly? I wondered. “We’ve had our mechanics look at it.” What did they do? I asked. “They certified it.” Yes, but what did they do? “I don’t know.” Can you find out? “No.” Is certified like a warranty? I inquired in disbelief. “No, that’s extra.” How long does your basic warranty last? “There is none, but it depends.”


Jamie Kitman


When I protested that in decades of buying cars, many from used car lots, I’d never seen anything as objectionable and strange as this, he got rude. “Maybe ‘coz you haven’t bought anything in a long time, Pops. Things have changed.” No, they haven’t, I replied. For one thing, you have a price in your ad that bears no relation to what you’re asking for now. That’s against the law. “Yes, but there’s always a certification fee.” Of course, there isn’t always such a fee, and when there is, it ought to come with some sort of extended warranty and a checklist of maintenance and repairs that have been done.


Unable to answer, the salesman passed me off to another salesman and we went back and forth along the same lines for what seemed like forever, when yet another salesman got on and said after much back and forth, “I need to speak to my manager, but if you finance it with us we can do it cheaper.” Sure, whatever, I said. I’ll give you $12,500. He refused, holding firm to $13,500. I refused back. He said, “If I can do $13,000, will you buy it?” Reluctantly I agreed. “First I have to speak to my manager.” Uh-oh, the old “let me speak to my manager” gambit. While I waited for the manager to emerge from his private lair, fearing that we’d not find another blue W205 C300 in the short time allotted to supply the car, I texted a friend in old Mercedes world, who said he’d check with another friend, who worked at Mercedes-Benz of Manhattan.


The New Jersey used car dealer manager got on the phone and I began reasonably, as is my practice. But then he started screaming at me. Not only would $13,000 not do it, he said after I pointed out that a hidden certification fee sounded pretty sketch, legally speaking. Then he dropped the bomb: $15,500 was their bottom line, plus sales tax and registration. I was apoplectic. Sensing the direction things were going, maybe it was time to go with a Plan B: I’d been frantically scrolling online dealer inventories and classified ads from the moment things had started going sideways. No way we were going to pay almost 50 percent extra over the listed price. There was another one about 200 miles away in Pennsylvania that could work, but would it be as represented? And could it all be done in time?


Jamie Kitman


Panic had long since set in. Should we knowingly get ripped off and buy the car we needed with an exorbitant undisclosed markup? Should I call the state’s attorney general? The Lord works in mysterious ways, for just then, I got a text from my friend. His pal at Mercedes-Benz of Manhattan had taken in a used, same-generation, correct-color-inside-and-out C300. It had more miles, but was fully detailed and super-clean, with a Carfax evidencing intensive maintenance throughout its life and a far, far superior price, including tax, registration, and a full tank of gas, delivered to our office. It wasn’t “certified,” but we weren’t being overcharged for it, either. The one thing I can certify is that I’d just encountered the creepiest used car dealership (I’m not mentioning their name, lest any of you attempt to try your luck) I’ve ever come across. Bill thanked them for their time, under his breath. And Mercedes of Manhattan proved as good as their word, less common in the world of used cars than neophytes might suppose.


In the world of doubling, doubling potential vendors is sometimes a good idea, too.


***


*A man of many pursuits (rock band manager, automotive journalist, concours judge, purveyor of picture cars for film and TV), Jamie Kitman lives and breathes vintage machines. His curious taste for interesting, oddball, and under-appreciated classics—which traffic through his Nyack, New York, warehouse—promises us an unending stream of delightful cars to discuss.* *For more Picture Car Confidential columns, click[here](https://www.hagerty.com/media/category/opinion/picture-car-confidential/) .* Follow Jamie Kitman on Instagram at @commodorehornblow; follow Octane Film Cars[@octanefilmcars](https://www.instagram.com/octanefilmcars) and at[www.octanefilmcars.com](https://www.octanefilmcars.com/) .
